revisions. [Supply tests](../tests/test_supply_integration.py) restrict markets to
the current ingredient request; fleet tests isolate courier assignment attempts.

**Limit:** this is exact filtered recall and explicit fact sharing. Cross-order
learning, vector recall, automatic consolidation and managed Memory Bank are not
implemented. Typed observations cannot override operational truth. Expiry removes
recall eligibility while retaining operator audit history; it is not a deletion
policy. [Memory contracts](AGENT-MEMORY.md).

## 4. Cost and tool admission

**Goal:** bound work before execution and retain the cost of uncertain attempts.

**Implemented proof:** [runtime tests](../tests/test_agent_runtime.py) exercise
concurrent durable reservations and exhausted limits. Optional judge tests verify
six calls/50,688 reserved tokens per run, with 8,448 tokens reserved per dispatch
and no new call charge for a saved-result replay. [Cloud request tests](../tests/test_cloud_ai.py)
enforce a bounded numeric context; [gateway tests](../tests/test_gateway_policy.py)
deny invalid or infeasible requests before model invocation.
[Search tests](../tests/test_supply_search_service.py) retain admission reservations
after provider failures. Default local scenarios invoke no model.

**Limit:** `model_usd: 0` is a schema literal, not a working paid-GCP dollar ceiling.
Per-run limits, one Cloud Run instance and scale-to-zero do not cap project spend.
A durable gateway-wide currency admission ledger and comparative live cost per
successful task remain missing. Provider regressions use injected responses;
historical live verification is documented separately. [GCP components](GCP-COMPONENTS.md).

## 5. Evaluations

**Goal:** make expected behavior explicit and reproduce both safe outcomes and
failure cases.

**Implemented proof:** the [scenario manifest](../data/evals/agent-scenarios.json)
declares twelve scenarios and 49 typed criteria. The
[evaluator](../src/delivery/scenario_evals.py) runs real scoped workers in disposable
local test worlds; [receipt validation](../src/delivery/scenario_report.py)
recomputes results and checks source/configuration/repeat hashes. Missing criteria
receive no credit, a later pass cannot erase an earlier failure, and source drift
fails reproducibility. [Evaluator tests](../tests/test_scenario_evals.py) verify
these rules, local-only database guards and cleanup after fixture failure.

**Limit:** these are fixed rules-based development regressions. They do not measure
held-out LLM quality, memory-strategy superiority, architecture comparisons,
production latency or business uplift. Historical live GCP system cases also
include deterministic preflight denials; their pass count is not a model accuracy
score. [Evaluation methodology](AGENT-EVALS.md), [dated cloud evidence](GCP-VERIFICATION.md).

## 6. Observability and replay

**Goal:** explain what work executed, what it observed and why the recorded
business state changed.

**Implemented proof:** decisions retain tool receipts, recalled fact IDs/revisions,
memory writes and event lineage. The operator can inspect complete order history.
Supply replay reconstructs business projections and detects fact-hash corruption;
[delivery-fact tests](../tests/test_supply_delivery_facts.py) retain world and
dispatcher changes even after a household order becomes terminal.
[Health reporting](../src/delivery/health.py) distinguishes missing, partial,
failed, stale and source-outdated receipts. Its
[tests](../tests/test_health.py) prevent incomplete evidence from appearing green.
The optional gateway emits structured decision, version, usage and timing records.

**Limit:** business replay and recorded explanations do not expose private model
reasoning. Complete OpenTelemetry propagation, Cloud Trace, production dashboards,
alert policies and declared cloud log retention are not configured. Reading local
health does not query current GCP deployment status. Use [health semantics](HEALTH.md)
and the [GCP operations runbook](GCP-AI.md) for their distinct evidence boundaries.
docs/DARK-STORE.md:
# Shelf to doorstep

Open Operations and choose **Start store demo**. One seeded synthetic order is
reserved from the catalogue, picked from physical shelves, packed, carried to the
loading dock, then delivered by a Madrid courier. **Picker breakdown** adds a
failure while the basket is in progress. The 60-second playback setting is a
target; a slower machine will take longer rather than skip physical steps.

The default view is an elevated cutaway. Cyan marks the selected order's shelf
faces and the current planned route. Green items are already in the basket.
Amber blocks show inaccessible cells. Use **Track worker** for a closer camera,
**Fit store** for the whole layout, or **Back to Madrid** to leave. **Follow this
order** returns to the city after physical courier collection; it ends at delivery
or cancellation. Select a robot or forklift label to follow that worker; the label
shows its actual task and the ground marker follows its route. Completed shifts
are labeled **shift complete**; start a store demo for live movement. Escape
leaves the store. On a focused 3D view, arrows orbit and
plus/minus zoom. All order facts and controls remain available without WebGL.

## Two environments, one order

`Environment` defines clock reads, ordered events, state reads and transactional
advance effects. `MadridCity` contains the original city physics; city-only runs
retain their minute tick and behavior. `DarkStore` shares its run ID and clock,
advances physical movement every ten simulated seconds, and records store frames.

`StoreLayoutConfig` generates four aisles, eight bays, three shelf levels, a cold
zone, a packing station and a loading dock by default. The sixty supermarket
catalogue products have two distinct pick faces each, including cold storage for
dairy, protein and frozen items. Opening physical stock is 24 units per SKU;
listing a product or expecting a truck never creates sellable stock.

Stock models sit inside the actual rack bounds on its raycast deck surfaces;
logical levels select usable decks rather than placing goods in mid-air. Shelf
and product instances share draw calls.

The renderer uses metre coordinates from this layout, not a separate visual
layout. Pick routes use deterministic shortest aisle paths, avoid rack cells and
blocked cells, and pick ambient goods before cold goods. This is a discrete
logistics simulation; it is not collision-accurate robotics physics. Worker
traffic does not yet reserve space against other workers.

## Agent decisions and bounded effects

The inventory role reuses `InventoryPolicy`, its typed reservation outcomes and
memory validation. A bound adapter permits only the selected run, store and
order. The fulfillment role adds a dark-store tool profile: route, pick, pack,
restock and handoff. Its policy observes available faces, workers and routes.
It does not branch on incident names. Both roles expose Agent Cards and execute
through the same A2A service used by the in-process test transport.

A route is only a plan. The environment emits an arrival event; a scoped tool
then checks reservation, quantity, position and elapsed time before changing
stock. A replacement picker must reach a broken robot before taking its basket.
The forklift first visits the dock and moves only confirmed backstock. Pack and
handoff tools refuse incomplete baskets. The dispatcher cannot assign an order
until the dock is ready.

Each decision is in the existing event/decision trail, with the same order ID.
New spans describe tools and environment advances; the observability system is
otherwise unchanged. The local policies use no model calls. The optional GCP
configuration includes separate inventory and fulfillment identities with
audience-bound A2A tokens; no cloud resources are started by this feature.

Store services use trusted database connections and bound application tools.
They do not claim the legacy inventory lab's separate SQL-login isolation.
Manifest profiles limit per-turn tools, per-run work, memory size and TTL.
Stock is conserved through cancellation, receipts, retries and disruptions.

## Store disruptions

| Event | Physical change | Decision left to the policy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Blocked aisle | Removes cells from the walk graph | Choose another face/path, or wait |
| Shelf out of stock | Removes a pick face; observed units move to unlocated backstock | Pick another face; forklift may restock a reachable face |
| Robot breakdown | Stops a robot at its last safe node | Recover its basket with an available picker |
| Late restock truck | Delays an expected receipt | Wait for actual receipt; never promise expected stock |

The existing Chaos API accepts these event kinds, `target` (a store ID or
`auto`) and optional `resource` (aisle, shelf, robot or shipment ID).
Explicit resources require an explicit store. Scenarios can provide an event
list; `random_store_events` uses a separate seeded stream so existing city
random sequences remain unchanged. Auto targets resolve from current store
load. Store decisions and events remain correlated to their order.

## API and recording

`POST /api/runs` accepts an optional `dark_store` configuration. Omit it for
the unchanged city simulation. `GET /api/runs/{run}/stores` returns current
layout, stock, worker routes, baskets and live load. Add `?at=120` to read the
last recorded frame at or before 120 simulated seconds. This endpoint is read
only and uses a consistent database snapshot.

For a short recording, submit the checked-in demo request:

```bash
curl -fsS http://localhost:8010/api/stores/demo \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data-binary @config/scenarios/store-demo.json
```

The UI's demo button makes the same request, selects `DS-0001`, and follows it.
An optional `chaos: true` inserts a robot failure. These are synthetic orders,
not real shoppers or customer communications. Live deployments retain global
authentication on all endpoints; public replay exposes no write APIs.

## Evidence and browser budget

`evals/store/scenarios.json` runs all four incidents twice over the official
A2A SDK. The gate recomputes pass criteria: delivered on time, complete basket,
dock recovery within 900 seconds, conserved stock, no orphan reservations, no
dead events, no paid calls, and identical normalized outcomes across repeats.
Robot recovery must be observed, and delayed trucks cannot be received early.

The seven NVIDIA SimReady models converted by
[codepawl](https://huggingface.co/datasets/codepawl/simready-glb) are
[CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Derivatives simplify
geometry, resize textures to 256 px, and use WebP and Meshopt compression.
The pinned source revision, original links, modifications and hashes are in
`web/vendor/simready/manifest.json`. The models total 920,992 bytes; models plus
the local Three.js loader stay below 4 MB. They load only when opening a store.
Failed models use boxes; failed WebGL uses the floor plan. Rendering is capped
at 30 fps and pixel ratio 1.5, skips unchanged frames, reduces resolution on slow
software GPUs, pauses in hidden views, and disposes its renderer
when closed. The original model geometry is visual evidence, not the simulation's
physical collision or navigation authority.

## Source index

- [Environment contract](../src/delivery/environment.py)
- [Madrid city adapter](../src/delivery/madrid_city.py)
- [Store layout and navigation](../src/delivery/store_layout.py)
- [Physical store state and effects](../src/delivery/dark_store.py)
- [Scoped store tools](../src/delivery/store_tools.py)
- [Inventory adapter and fulfillment policy](../src/delivery/store_agents.py)
- [Measured recovery runner](../src/delivery/store_evals.py)
- [Frozen store scenarios](../evals/store/scenarios.json)
- [Asset provenance and byte budget](../web/vendor/simready/manifest.json)
docs/DELIVERY-FLOW.md:
# Local basket-to-delivery slice

This document describes the preserved first delivery slice and its regression
backend. The Delivery grid UI is retired and `/delivery-lab` redirects to Operations.
Saved legacy runs remain available through the delivery APIs. See also the
[expanded fleet recovery scenario](FLEET-RECOVERY.md).
The existing `/lab` last-unit/crash/delayed-supply scenario remains available.
Both use the same local factory, permissions, scoped tools, private memory,
durable budgets and fenced event-processing transaction.

```sh
docker compose exec -T app delivery delivery-demo
```

This runs a synthetic one-item basket on the 10×10 city, exports an evidence bundle
to ignored `artifacts/delivery-<run>.json`, and makes no model or provider calls.
Recorded evidence includes role boundaries, budgets, decision inputs, queue lineage
and consistent checkpoints. It is not a complete replay engine.

## Queue-only lifecycle

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[Scenario] -->|basket.requested| Q[(Postgres queue)]
    Q --> I[Inventory: own store]
    I -->|basket.reserved| Q
    Q --> F[Fulfillment: own store]
    F -->|basket.ready| Q
    Q --> D[Dispatcher: run fleet]
    D -->|delivery.assigned| Q
    W[Trusted physical world] -->|delivery.arrived| Q
    D -->|delivery.completed| Q
```

1. Inventory reserves one confirmed unit and emits an opaque basket reference.
2. Fulfillment validates the live own-store reservation, decrements on-hand and
   reserved stock together, writes one ledger movement and creates a ready job.
   The reservation becomes `picked`; repeated picking has no second effect.
3. Dispatch reads the logistics projection and selects an available bike. It
   plans connected roads from the courier's node through the store to the customer.
   The command independently validates endpoints, every directed edge and travel
   time, and atomically claims the courier. Concurrent jobs cannot claim one bike.
4. The world engine advances simulation time and the courier along those edges.
   It marks collection/in-transit/arrival and publishes `delivery.arrived`, linked
   to the assignment event. Agents cannot move the clock or manufacture arrival.
5. Dispatch confirms delivery only after authoritative arrival, releases the
   courier, marks the basket delivered and publishes the final queued result.

For seed 42, the bike travels from depot node 22 through pickup node 2 to customer
node 88. Collection occurs at simulation second 138 and arrival at second 1,016.
The UI uses individual edge travel times when placing the courier.

## Enforced role boundaries

| Identity | Permitted facts and actions | Denied access |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `inventory:store-N` | Own-store stock, reservations, replenishment and catalogue projection | Fulfillment commands, dispatch commands and other store/run state |
| `fulfillment:store-N` | Own reserved basket's SKU, quantity, expiry and picking status; atomic pick; queued ready handoff | Raw stock/catalogue/world/fleet tables, other stores, route assignment and delivery confirmation |
| `dispatcher:fleet` | This run's opaque ready jobs, road graph and courier availability; assign and confirm after arrival | Product identities, quantities, prices, stock, picking and fulfillment memory |

Five inventory and five fulfillment identities plus one dispatcher are provisioned
through separate non-superuser logins. Only three perform work in this small demo;
the other identities make the boundaries inspectable. Role namespaces are distinct
keys in the existing binding/budget/memory tables: inventory retains `store-N`,
fulfillment uses `fulfillment:store-N`, and dispatch uses `dispatcher:fleet`.

New roles have no direct table grants on inventory, fulfillment jobs or fleet.
Fixed security-definer projections/commands bind access to authenticated identity;
each command has role-specific execution grants. Event row security limits incoming
topics and destinations, and allows inspection of the identity's own outgoing
handoffs. Trusted destination rules route handoffs; policies cannot choose arbitrary
agents or stores. All messages retain the basket trace and parent event ID.

Definitions in `config/agents/{inventory,fulfillment,dispatcher}` are frozen per
run. JSON and soul text cannot grant another role's tools. Private expiring memory
and budget tickets use the same runtime as inventory. Default agent caps remain
100 attempts, eight slots per attempt, 400 slots per run and zero model spend;
the aggregate run cap remains 500 attempts and 2,000 slots.

The operator API/UI, fixed Python implementations and host are trusted, as documented
in [the foundation](AGENT-FOUNDATION.md). This is not an arbitrary-code sandbox.

## Verification and limits

The full Linux suite passes 76 tests, including nine new lifecycle/permission tests;
an additional operator API contract test passes separately. Ruff and mypy pass.
Chrome checks cover delivered stock, 100 nodes/360 roads, role boundaries, evidence
download, completed-run reload and desktop/mobile layout.

Tests include expired reservations, rollback of picking and its outgoing handoff
together, retry without duplicate consumption, forbidden direct table reads,
cross-store fulfillment denial, role switching, forged producers/destinations,
budget modification, hidden product data in dispatch, fabricated arrival,
disconnected routes and concurrent courier claims. Existing actual worker-crash
and Madrid regressions continue to pass.

This is a single-item, single-courier happy-path delivery slice. Continuous worker
supervision, controller restart recovery, cancellations/returns, arbitrary basket
expiry scheduling, cargo/energy constraints, traffic disruptions, multi-basket
dispatch waiting, architecture comparisons and full replay remain future work.
The world controller polls authoritative jobs as physical state; it does not call
another agent to complete work. Evaluated agents communicate through events only.

# Dispatch from the street

The Madrid map now defaults to rolling maximum-cardinality, minimum-cost
assignment. Couriers start across nearby stores and remain at their last drop-off
until another job is assigned. A home-base label is administrative affiliation,
not a return instruction. Everything runs locally without model calls.

## What was wrong

The previous dispatcher minimized completion ETA and broke ties by courier ID.
Food preparation can make several completion ETAs identical: the nearby courier
waits longer at the restaurant, while a farther courier spends that time driving.
The lexical tie then selects `01`, even though it wastes empty kilometres.

The backend already retained the customer's node after delivery. The apparent
return on the map came from resetting animation on duplicate snapshots: the UI
projected movement ahead, then drew the same older position again. Six couriers
also began at each hub, obscuring individual markers. One monotonic display clock
now supplies both rendering and animation; duplicate polls do not reset it.
Projection remains bounded to one 60-second simulation tick. SQL snapshots use a
short, read-only repeatable-read transaction so clock, routes and positions agree.

## Assignment algorithm

At each queue-triggered dispatch opportunity, the dispatcher reads at most 100
pending orders and 100 eligible idle couriers. Arrivals already share the city's
60-second clock; no extra artificial batching delay is introduced.

1. Construct directed road routes from each courier's **current** node, through
   the store, to the customer. Never substitute the home-base node.
2. Exclude unreachable routes, insufficient energy reserves and shift overruns.
3. Solve the feasible bipartite graph with exact maximum flow and minimum cost.
   First maximize served orders; then prioritize the earliest deadlines; then
   minimize economic cost for that served order set. Each courier and order may
   participate in one assignment. Charging lateness only to selected jobs would
   otherwise make an overdue order increasingly unattractive when capacity is
   tight. Bounded binary priority weights prevent that starvation trap.
4. For equal total economic cost, prefer longer-idle couriers, then fewer completed
   jobs, then a seeded, non-lexical tie. Fairness does not override road economics.
5. Commit reservations, decision evidence, the queue handoff and event ACK
   atomically. The existing active-order uniqueness constraint still protects
   against competing dispatchers. Couriers accept work through the queue.

The score uses generalized seconds:

```text
completion_duration
+ 20 × lateness
+ empty_pickup_travel_time
+ marginal_vehicle_cost × 3600 / 12
```

The €12/hour conversion, lateness and empty-time weights are editable in the
validated `dispatch` object on `POST /api/runs`. Each run stores a frozen policy.
The UI exposes the two main choices: economic versus legacy dispatch, and staying
at drop-off versus experimental demand-aware repositioning. The legacy arm keeps
the original earliest-completion/ID rule for controlled comparisons. Historical
runs with no policy retain their original interpretation.

Each assignment records its source node, pickup distance, ETA, cost components,
eligible count, batch size and up to five alternative courier scores. An
individually second-best match can be selected when it improves the whole batch.
Inspect this under a courier's recorded evidence on the map.

## Empty travel costs something

Actual movement updates distance, empty distance, normalized energy and marginal
operating cost every tick, including unfinished trips. Cumulative per-leg meters
make repeated ticks and crash replay idempotent. Preparation waits add no distance.
A completed delivery adds the existing €1 task fee once.

| Vehicle | Synthetic marginal cost | Normalized energy per km |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Bike | €0.12/km | 1.5 |
| Moto | €0.28/km | 0.7 |
| Van | €0.55/km | 0.4 |

These are simulation assumptions, not measured fuel prices or driver pay. Time
has value in the optimization objective; hourly wages are not charged in the
operating-cost ledger. Whole-fleet cost per completed delivery includes actual
empty repositioning and partial travel. Historical runs predate these meters:
their original completed-task cost remains an estimate and missing empty meters
are displayed as unavailable rather than zero.

## Repositioning is optional and conservative

**Stay at drop-off is the default.** The experimental alternative uses only orders
observed within the previous 30 minutes. It estimates next-15-minute demand,
checks the coverage supplied by other idle couriers and already reserved
destinations, and proposes a move only when the estimated reduction in pickup
time exceeds travel expense plus a two-minute margin.

Moves have a distance cap, cooldown, energy reserve and shift/run horizon. At
most two are proposed per event, and none while orders are still pending. A
durable `courier.reposition` event must be acknowledged before movement begins.
Delayed handoffs rebase departure to acceptance time or cancel when the move no
longer fits. Ordinary delivery assignments also rebase departure and remaining
preparation wait; an infeasible acceptance releases the order for a fresh,
versioned assignment. Every metre consumes energy and cost. There is no teleport or
automatic hub return. Stores with fewer than two observed orders are not targets.

Coverage treats another moving courier's reserved destination as future supply;
this simple forecast can be wrong. Repositioning can cost more than waiting. It
stays optional and is evaluated separately rather than advertised as an automatic
improvement.

## Two city runtimes, explicit boundaries

| Runtime | Implemented here | Remaining work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Madrid baseline (`/`) | Fleet batch optimization, marginal economics, distributed starts, optional real repositioning, monotonic movement | Traffic-dependent ETA, mode-specific access, bundled multi-stop trips, reassignment during empty travel, calibrated costs and demand forecasting |
| Restaurant/delivery labs | Shared matching primitive for the one basket visible to the role; directed traffic-weighted routes; actual live/custody node; stable basket-specific ties; common-leg search reuse | A scoped multi-order projection and economics ledger before fleet-wide batching/repositioning |

The lab change does not grant access to raw fleet, jobs or another agent's memory.
Its planner receives the existing authorized projection. A global restaurant
optimizer needs a separately reviewed projection/tool, not broader SQL grants.
The Madrid graph still uses fixed mode speeds and a shared directed drivable
network; the lab's simulated traffic weights are not silently applied to it.
Soft lateness penalties do not guarantee every deadline under overloaded demand.
The bounded pending window takes the first 100 deadlines. A backlog of 100
infeasible orders can hide feasible later orders; paged candidate search and an
explicit unsatisfiable-order policy remain future work.

## Reproduce and inspect

Run only against the dedicated local test database. No provider keys or cloud
credentials are needed:

```bash
docker compose exec -T app python scripts/benchmark_dispatch.py \
  --seed 42 --seed 73 --include-reposition \
  --output artifacts/dispatch-comparison.json
node --test scripts/test_courier_motion.cjs
docker compose exec -T app python -m pytest \
  tests/test_dispatch_optimizer.py tests/test_workflow_dispatch.py \
  tests/test_economic_dispatch.py
```

The comparison pairs the same graph, initial fleet and seeded demand; it clears
the route cache between arms and saves complete snapshots. Its wall time includes
SQL, queue handling and Python overhead; it is not a solver-only latency claim.
Costs and job spread accompany completion and lateness so an apparent saving
cannot hide dropped work. The two seeded days are examples, not a statistical
claim about production performance. See the committed [comparison receipt](evidence/dispatch-comparison.json).

Final-policy results on the pinned road graph:

| Seed | Policy | On time / orders | Empty km | Operating cost | Jobs per courier |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 42 | Legacy, stay | 247 / 247 | 336.980 | €453.96 | 2–35 |
| 42 | Deadline + cost, stay | 247 / 247 | 253.930 | €391.52 | 4–22 |
| 42 | Deadline + cost, reposition | 247 / 247 | 267.316 | €400.76 | 5–22 |
| 73 | Legacy, stay | 248 / 248 | 357.692 | €470.45 | 0–37 |
| 73 | Deadline + cost, stay | 248 / 248 | 260.721 | €401.38 | 5–24 |
| 73 | Deadline + cost, reposition | 248 / 248 | 279.793 | €410.09 | 6–24 |

Across both days, staying with the new matcher reduces empty travel by 25.915%
and simulated total operating cost by 14.227%, with all 495 deliveries on time
and zero dead letters. Repositioning adds 87.376 km of movement and costs more
than staying on these days, which supports keeping it optional. No paid calls
were made. The receipt's source hash matches the final dispatch code; an earlier
exploratory run was superseded after the deadline and handoff fixes.

Tests cover exhaustive small-graph assignment oracles, a greedy assignment trap,
input permutations, bounded batches, equal-ETA near/far regression, staying at
drop-off, partial and duplicate ticks, waiting, one completion fee, delayed/cancelled
relocation, observed-only history, distance/energy/horizon bounds, scoped lab
traffic routes and the animation rewind. Python cases appear under City &
fulfillment in `/health`; the six Node movement cases also run in CI.
The full local suite passed 704 Python tests, Ruff, mypy over 57 modules, twelve
agent scenarios repeated twice with matching business outcomes, and six offline
judge cases. HTTP checks verified local assets and control bindings. A browser
visual review was unavailable because the computer-use service exposed no browsers.

## Why this approach

Uber publicly describes matching nearby requests in short batches to reduce
collective waiting rather than immediately selecting the nearest driver. Its
older Eats engineering account also explains why preparation time and pickup
waiting matter. This project adopts those public principles with an inspectable
operations-research algorithm. It does not reproduce Uber's private production
model or claim state-of-the-art delivery performance. Research on dynamic pickup
and delivery also studies reoptimization with travel and tardiness costs; learned
lookahead and multi-stop search are future extensions here.

Sources reviewed 2026-10-29: [Uber matching](https://www.uber.com/au/en/marketplace/matching/),
[Uber Eats trip optimization (2018)](https://www.uber.com/us/en/blog/uber-eats-trip-optimization/),
[dynamic pickup/delivery cost approximation research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.01915).

Implementation: [matcher](../src/delivery/dispatch_optimizer.py),
[policy](../src/delivery/dispatch_policy.py),
[dispatcher and courier](../src/delivery/agents.py),
[repositioning](../src/delivery/dispatch_reposition.py),
[scoped lab planner](../src/delivery/workflow_policy.py),
[road geometry and progress](../src/delivery/world.py),
[snapshot and initial fleet](../src/delivery/simulation.py),
[migration](../sql/migrations/027_economic_dispatch.sql),
[comparison script](../scripts/benchmark_dispatch.py),
[matcher tests](../tests/test_dispatch_optimizer.py),
[economics and recovery tests](../tests/test_economic_dispatch.py),
[lab planner tests](../tests/test_workflow_dispatch.py).

# Durable inference without open database transactions

The optional recovery judge uses three committed phases: prepare a request,
invoke and save a result, then apply it against fresh authoritative state. The
network call has no open worker database connection or transaction. Local rules,
role scope, leases and business constraints remain the execution authority.

This chapter describes the new local request/result protocol. It does not deploy
GCP resources or demonstrate live model quality. Crash verification uses a fake
provider and real worker-process termination; no paid calls are needed.

## Execution and transaction boundaries

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant A as Scoped judge worker
    participant D as PostgreSQL
    participant P as Bounded provider
    A->>D: Prepare immutable request under fenced lease
    D-->>A: Commit request, context and local proposal
    A->>D: Commit dispatch marker and call allowance
    Note over A,D: Close connection before remote I/O
    A->>P: Invoke with sanitized numeric facts
    P-->>A: Schema-validated verdict
    A->>D: Save result in a short fenced transaction
    D-->>A: Commit saved result
    A->>D: Re-read current state and validate saved proposal
    Note over A,D: Apply effects, memory, outbox and ACK atomically
    D-->>A: Commit completed event
```

The preparatory snapshot comes from the authenticated incoming event, the judge's
scoped tools and selective memory recall. It includes a locally computed courier
and route proposal. The durable record binds that input to its run, namespace,
source event, frozen role definition and endpoint. The cloud receives only the
existing numeric allowlist and the number of recalled facts; memory bodies,
customer names, local identifiers and raw route coordinates remain local.

Before dispatch admission, the worker rechecks context, simulated time and recalled
facts. It also verifies enough tool slots remain for the fresh recall and five
application operations. Known-stale preparation is denied before spending a call.
After the dispatch marker commits, all worker SQL connections are closed. Token
acquisition and the provider request happen outside the transaction. A separate
short transaction saves the validated response. `Queue.process` then starts its
usual effects transaction, reloads the authoritative event, validates its fence,
reads current business state and consumes the saved result. The deterministic
policy does not call the provider from inside this transaction.

## Recovery policy

| Durable state at restart | Recovery | Additional provider call |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Prepared, dispatch not claimed | A live fenced worker may claim dispatch | One admitted call |
| In flight under another still-active worker | Leave ownership intact; report busy | None |
| Dispatch committed, previous worker died | Record an unknown outcome and fail closed after reclaim | None |
| Response received but result not saved | Outcome remains unknown after worker death | None |
| Validated result saved, effects not committed | Reuse the saved result and revalidate current facts | None |
| Effects transaction crashed before commit | Roll back effects, memory, outgoing events and ACK; reuse result on reclaim | None |
| Applied and acknowledged | Work is complete; a stale worker cannot apply again | None |
| Legacy call with no durable snapshot | Preserve its allowance and deny; old inputs cannot be proven compatible | None |

Prepared requests and saved results are keyed by the source event, not by a queue
delivery attempt. Reclaiming an event therefore does not create a second model
call or reserve a second model allowance. A genuinely new decision event remains
a separate admission. Reservations for uncertain calls are retained.

An approval is a proposal about the saved facts. The application phase rechecks
the current job, delivery attempt, custody, courier availability, route and
deadline. A stale or incompatible proposal is rejected. The model cannot invent
a replacement route or override the SQL feasibility gates.

## What safe retries can and cannot mean

There is no distributed transaction between PostgreSQL and a model provider.
The worker cannot distinguish a crash immediately before sending from a crash
after the provider accepted the request but before its response was recorded.
A stable local request key does not prove provider-side deduplication or
exactly-once billing. The implementation deliberately avoids automatic resend
across this uncertain boundary.

This policy trades availability for bounded spend and safe business effects.
Unknown outcomes require a denial or an explicit future reconciliation workflow;
they are not silently retried until an answer arrives. A future provider that
offers an idempotent request API and durable result lookup could support a
different recovery policy, after its behavior and billing semantics are tested.

## Isolation, budgets and evidence

Raw request and history tables are not agent-readable. Narrow SQL functions
derive scope from `session_user`, require the current event lease and budget
ticket, and fence dispatch/result/application transitions. A stale worker cannot
overwrite a newer terminal outcome. Recorded errors use safe codes, not provider
exception messages that might contain credentials.

The original per-run model call and token limits still apply. Dispatch admission
charges a request once; reusing its saved result does not charge another call.
This remains a call/token allowance, not a project-wide currency cap. The
existing GCP gateway and Terraform resources do not change for this local work.

The [crash suite](../tests/test_inference_crash_recovery.py) checks physical process
death at the phase boundaries, saved-result
reuse, uncertain-outcome denial, lease fencing, concurrent ownership, unchanged
business effects and the absence of worker SQL transactions during provider I/O.
Use the [health dashboard](HEALTH.md) for fresh source-linked test evidence and
[architecture decisions](ARCHITECTURE-DECISIONS.md) for the remaining trade-offs.
The implementation lives in [durable_inference.py](../src/delivery/durable_inference.py),
the [new SQL state machine](../sql/migrations/016_durable_inference.sql),
the [shared worker](../src/delivery/agent_runtime.py) and
[receipt-only policy](../src/delivery/fleet_policy.py).

# Enterprise agents on GCP: architecture and delivery decisions

Reviewed against source and Google documentation on **2026-10-28**. This is the
client architecture guide. [Agent implementation](AGENT-IMPLEMENTATION.md) explains
the exact executable worker; [GCP components](GCP-COMPONENTS.md) inventories every
declared cloud resource; [GCP operations](GCP-AI.md) covers start/status/stop.
Recommendations below are **proposed** unless explicitly marked implemented.
This review did not deploy infrastructure, inspect credentials or invoke a model.

## Client objective and current decision

Build a delivery/sourcing system whose agents can make bounded decisions while
inventory, consent, custody, approvals and money remain enforceable business rules.
Use the local synthetic city as a reproducible client test environment. Introduce
paid inference only for a declared decision task and promote it only when measured
benefit exceeds added latency, failures and cost.

Implemented today: custom Python/Postgres role workers, queued cooperation,
authenticated scopes, typed selective recall, budgets and local scenario evals.
The optional cloud component is an IAM-authenticated **Cloud Run recovery judge
calling a Google publisher model through Vertex REST**. It can veto a locally
computed candidate; it cannot invent a route, change stock or execute a delivery.
The [restaurant adapter](ADK-RESTAURANT.md) now runs Google ADK locally with granular
tools and an explicitly offline model double. Managed Agent Runtime, Memory Bank
and Agent Gateway are not deployed; restaurant Gemini calls are not enabled.

Google's current product documentation uses **Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform**
and **Agent Runtime**; older Agent Engine/Vertex AI names and API resource names
remain visible in documentation and integrations. Separate the framework, hosting,
model API and governance layers when choosing components. Google documents both
Cloud Run and managed runtime options; our selection depends on the client's
operational and governance requirements, not a requirement to use every service.
[Google architecture component guide](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/choose-agentic-ai-architecture-components).

## Choose the runtime by workload

Before platform selection, agree the task and unsafe outcomes, expected demand,
deadline/latency SLO, acceptable cost per successful task, tenant/data boundaries,
processing region, retention, operator approval rules and RTO/RPO. Assign owners
for policy, data access, release approval, incident response and billing. The local
city supplies test incidents; it does not define an enterprise client's SLOs.

| Option | Use when | Our decision / limitation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cloud Run service | Bounded, stateless HTTP decisions; variable demand; explicit container/network controls | Implemented for the judge, with local durable inference phases. Candidate for a separately evaluated ADK pilot |
| Cloud Run job | Finite evaluations, imports or migrations | Proposed for an explicitly cloud-enabled benchmark; current benchmark stays local |
| Cloud Run worker pool | Continuous pull consumers without an inbound HTTP API | Candidate for production queue workers; provisioned instance lifetime is billable |
| Managed Agent Runtime | Managed agent hosting, sessions, identity/governance and lifecycle capabilities materially reduce client operations | Evaluate against the same workload and permissions before choosing it |
| GKE | Client already needs Kubernetes-specific networking, scheduling or isolation controls | No current requirement; owning a cluster is not an agent prerequisite |

Cloud Run services can scale to zero; jobs and worker pools have different
lifecycle/billing behavior. Moving an in-process API background task onto a
request-billed service does not make it a durable worker. Choose a supervised
consumer or a bounded task, with external state and restart-safe ownership.
[Cloud Run agent resource choices](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/ai-agents),
[billing behavior](https://docs.cloud.google.com/run/docs/configuring/billing-settings).

The local restaurant implementation pins ADK 2.13.0 and compatible SDK dependencies.
Keep our role definition, authenticated tool boundary and queue protocol as the
business contract; ADK becomes the reasoning adapter. Do not replace those
contracts with a prompt or a framework's implicit shared state. Google's
[ADK and Cloud Run reference architecture](https://docs.cloud.google.com/architecture/single-agent-ai-system-adk-cloud-run)
provides a deployment reference; it is not a claim that this repository already
implements that architecture.

## A reusable enterprise agent contract

The proposed reasoning adapter should accept a validated definition containing
purpose, role/version, instructions, supported event schemas, tool references,
memory policy, numeric limits, deadline behavior and escalation route. Tenant/run
scope comes from a trusted deployment/event binding. Configurations and model
proposals cannot choose arbitrary URLs, credentials, recipients or tools.

Construct one adapter for one trust boundary: load frozen definition → resolve
approved tool wrappers → build scoped context → invoke bounded reasoning →
validate output → request domain execution. Reuse the image/factory and change
approved definitions. Adding a new role still requires domain permissions and
evaluation coverage. Several ADK subagents in one process do not receive distinct
IAM identities merely because their prompts have different names.

Domain tool endpoints must authenticate the workload and independently authorize
tenant, role, current order and operation. For MCP or A2A, implement authenticated,
schema-versioned adapters; accepted business messages become durable queue events.
Do not add direct agent transfer/shared conversational state that bypasses the
project's queue-only cooperation rule. Tool calls to a domain service and messages
to another agent are different operations. Google's safety guidance reinforces
enforcement in tool context/callbacks rather than relying on instructions alone.
[ADK safety and security](https://adk.dev/safety/).

## Identity, isolation and governance

**Implemented:** separate caller and runtime service accounts; caller-specific
Cloud Run invocation; a custom runtime role with only
`aiplatform.endpoints.predict`; keyless ADC/impersonation; scoped PostgreSQL agent
logins. The endpoint is internet-reachable with IAM authentication. There is no
private VPC ingress or generic tenant authorization gateway in the current module.

**For a client deployment:** separate dev/staging/production ownership and state,
deployer and runtime identities, and role trust boundaries. Reject public
invocation. Decide ingress/egress, residency, key management, incident access and
retention with the client before selecting networking controls. Identity grants
permission to reach a service; business authorization still decides which store,
order, event lease and operation the caller may access.

For restricted client data, assess private connectivity and VPC Service Controls
against supported services/locations; a perimeter complements IAM to reduce
exfiltration risk. Select CMEK only where supported and required. Test denied
egress and approved access explicitly. An EU-hosted Cloud Run service using a
global model endpoint is not an EU-only processing guarantee. These controls are
proposed, with no network perimeter or CMEK resource in the current module.
[VPC Service Controls](https://cloud.google.com/security/vpc-service-controls).

When choosing managed Agent Runtime, evaluate **Agent Identity** rather than
assuming a shared default service account is sufficiently narrow. Its identity is
tied to the deployed runtime resource, not every local role object. Current docs
describe runtime-bound credentials and default grants including
`roles/aiplatform.agentDefaultAccess` and `roles/aiplatform.agentContextEditor`;
review those grants and keep context-aware credential protections enabled.
These features are not retroactively provided by our existing Cloud Run service.
[Agent Identity behavior and defaults](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/scale/runtime/agent-identity).

For governed tool estates, evaluate **Agent Registry**, **Agent Gateway** and
**Model Armor** against the chosen runtime and client policy. Registry describes
approved agents/tools; gateway enforcement and content inspection complement
IAM and domain authorization. They do not make untrusted tool output safe by
definition. Confirm runtime support, launch stage, region, pricing and Terraform
coverage before adoption; include allow/deny and injection tests in acceptance.
No such resources are currently provisioned.
[Agent platform layers](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/agents),
[gateway deployment options](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/govern/gateways/agent-gateway-overview).

Terraform ownership is an adoption gate for each proposed service. Verify that the
selected provider/API can create, import, plan, update and delete the runtime and
its dependent billable resources. An SDK or ADK CLI deployment is not automatically
Terraform-owned. Defer an unsupported component or design a reviewed declarative
lifecycle module; document session/memory data retention and cleanup separately.

Use Workload Identity Federation for production CI/external workloads instead of
downloaded service-account keys or a human ADC mount. Bind federation to the
approved repository/workflow/environment and trusted claims, and separate plan
from approved apply permissions. The current GitHub workflow tests local Docker;
it is not a cloud deployment pipeline. For third-party secrets, introduce Secret
Manager only with narrow access and lifecycle ownership; Gemini on GCP needs
workload credentials, not a hard-coded model API key.
[Google pipeline identity guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/best-practices-for-using-service-accounts-in-deployment-pipelines),
[federation setup](https://docs.cloud.google.com/iam/docs/workload-identity-federation-with-deployment-pipelines).

## Durable execution: implemented local phases and remaining gaps

The local worker atomically commits state, memory, decision, outbox and ACK.
The optional judge now uses a separate durable request/result protocol:

1. In a short fenced transaction, save the authenticated event, scoped observations,
   relevant recall, frozen identity and local proposal as an immutable request.
2. Commit a single-dispatch marker and call/token admission, then close the worker
   database connection before authentication or provider I/O.
3. Save a validated result in its own short transaction. Reclaiming the same event
   reuses that result. A crash with an in-flight outcome fails closed rather than
   resending: the provider does not offer a proven exactly-once billing contract.
4. In the effects transaction, re-read current state and compare the saved facts,
   proposal, recall and time. SQL independently rechecks feasibility; effects,
   memory, outgoing events and ACK commit together or roll back together.

See [durable inference and crash boundaries](DURABLE-INFERENCE.md). This is a local
single-dispatch ledger, not a shared gateway-wide currency cap or a durable cloud
supervisor. Prepared work can resume; saved results can be reapplied safely;
uncertain invocations retain their charge and need explicit reconciliation rather
than hidden retries. Future distributed completion wakeups and tracing propagation
must preserve the same queue-only contract.

Add durable controller ownership/checkpoints and an orphan-identity reaper.
Kill the controller and the inference worker separately; prove recovery before
claiming cloud fault tolerance. Move state to Cloud SQL only after testing actual
managed-Postgres migration privileges, non-owner RLS, extensions, pooling,
connection limits, backup/restore and failover. Local superuser provisioning is
not evidence that unchanged migrations work in a managed service.

If Pub/Sub is added, start with wakeups from a transactional outbox while SQL
retains priority, virtual due time and domain idempotency. A full transport change
requires an inbox/outbox design and new failure tests. Pub/Sub's exactly-once
feature is regional and pull-subscription-specific; it does not provide an atomic
transaction with our stock tables or exactly-once external model charging.
[Pub/Sub delivery semantics](https://docs.cloud.google.com/pubsub/docs/exactly-once-delivery).

## Canonical state, sessions and memory

| Layer | Current implementation | Client design rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Business truth | Transactional PostgreSQL stock/orders/consent/custody | SQL constraints and version checks remain authoritative |
| Conversation/session | Correlated queued order/call events and frozen run settings | Persist outside a scaled stateless runtime; derive user/tenant identity from authentication |
| Selective recall | Typed facts scoped to role/current order; request/attempt filters; provenance/expiry/history | Authorization filters precede retrieval; bound bytes and recall cost |
| Cross-session knowledge | Not implemented | Evaluate managed Memory Bank or a scoped PostgreSQL/vector design only for a measurable task |
| Audit | Decision/tool/memory receipts and replay facts | Separate agent recall access from operator audit access and retention |

Managed sessions and Memory Bank can reduce custom context management, but neither
replaces transactional business state. A scope label or semantic match is not an
authorization check. Evaluate extraction quality, poisoned/stale facts, consent,
deletion/export, region and metering before sending client history to a managed
memory service. Our cloud judge currently receives a **memory count**, not memories.
[Memory Bank capabilities](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/scale/memory-bank).

Current TTL expires recall eligibility, not physical audit retention. Production
needs a declared wall-clock retention/deletion policy for facts, revisions, traces,
backups and model context. Add vector recall only if exact structured retrieval
fails a held-out task; then compare recall quality, leakage, latency and tokens.

## Model choice and cost controls

The historically verified model is `gemini-3.5-flash-lite`; Terraform requires an
explicit model/location, and the gateway assumes `MINIMAL` thinking is supported.
Do not swap in a newer model family without checking generation settings, regional
support, release status and rerunning the same evals. Record returned model version,
image/prompt/schema/role/fixture hashes, location and pricing date. Monitor model
retirement. A model alias is not a guarantee of identical future outputs.
[Model specifications and lifecycle](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/models/gemini/3-5-flash-lite).

Choose the least expensive model that passes the client's quality and latency
gates. For this numeric feasibility task, deterministic rules may remain the best
choice: the LLM's business benefit is unproven. A future ambiguous substitution or
incident-review task needs an approved evidence contract and human-calibrated
rubric before a larger model is justified.

Current standard global text rates checked 2026-10-28 for 3.5 Flash-Lite are $0.30
input and $2.50 output/reasoning per million tokens. At the caller's 8,192 + 256
reserved-token envelope, one illustrative maximum-envelope generation is
`(8192 × 0.30 + 256 × 2.50) / 1,000,000 = $0.0030976`; six are $0.0185856.
This is arithmetic for that SKU/location, **not a project-wide cost ceiling**.
It excludes compute, storage, logs, network, other clients and uncertain requests.
A local timeout or gateway 502 can follow a successful billable Vertex response.
[Current model pricing](https://cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/generative-ai/pricing).

Before exposing more callers, add a **durable gateway admission ledger** keyed by
tenant/project/window and business request ID. Reserve worst-case gross currency,
input/output/reasoning tokens and calls before inference; reject exhaustion and
reconcile actual usage. Account for the complete prompt/schema/context and every
attempt, including auth/SDK retry behavior. Current local `model_usd: 0`, Cloud Run
maximum instances and per-run call reservations do not implement this ledger.

Configure actual/forecast billing alerts and a tested containment action, with
an owner for reconciliation. Budget alerts are not an immediate spending cap.
Current Google documentation also lists service-scoped spend-cap budgets for
Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI) and Cloud Run, among eligible services. Assess
eligibility and manage separate project/service caps in Terraform before enabling
them. They are not deployed here. Enforcement is not instant; in-flight requests
and reporting latency can produce payable overages. They are not an all-project
ceiling. Use admission controls and explicit shutdown alongside billing signals.
[Google budget behavior](https://docs.cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/budgets),
[Spend-cap scope and limitations](https://docs.cloud.google.com/billing/docs/how-to/budgets-spend-caps).

## Evals, observability and release gates

The current [local role battery](AGENT-EVALS.md) records 12/12 cases and 49/49
criteria across two matching seed-731 runs, plus 392 passing tests. It exercises
rules-based agents and scoped SQL identities. The separate historical live GCP
eval achieved 6/6 system cases with **one model answer and five preflight denials**;
an earlier missing-facts model approval is retained in the evidence. Neither is
a held-out model benchmark or proof of business uplift.

For a client, evaluate both final task success and the tool trajectory. Use a
frozen family-separated tuning/holdout split, repeat model cases, and compare
rules-only vs model-assisted runs on the same incident schedules. A second LLM may
help assess explanations with human calibration; it cannot replace the hard
feasibility/tenancy oracle. Check the launch stage and price of the selected
managed evaluation feature before using it in a contractual release process.
[Google agent evaluation dimensions](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/models/evaluation-agents).

| Release gate | Evidence required before production |
| --- | --- |
| Isolation/safety | Zero executed hard-rule violations or cross-scope disclosures in declared adversarial cases; rejected attempts remain visible |
| Decision quality | Approve/deny confusion matrix, false denials, explanation support and human-reviewed disagreements on held-out incidents |
| Business outcome | Paired on-time delivery/recovery, abandoned work and operator effort, with predeclared tolerances and uncertainty |
| Performance | End-to-end cold/warm p50/p95/p99, queue age, timeout/429/5xx rates and late-result rejection against client deadline slack |
| Cost | Actual usage and gross currency per decision/successful recovery, uncertain reservations and concurrent admission tests |
| Recovery | Worker/controller failure, duplicate delivery, stale proposal, restore and rollback drills |
| Reproducibility | Frozen inputs, source/model/prompt/role versions, policy and architecture assignment, sanitized trace/eval receipts |

Add OpenTelemetry spans linking order → event → worker → tool → model, exported to
Cloud Trace/Logging/Monitoring with explicit redaction, sampling and retention.
Track budget admission, safety denials, feasible retries incorrectly denied,
queue/dead-letter growth and on-time delivery; an always-deny model can have perfect
uptime. Gateway stdout and local event inspection exist; complete distributed
tracing, alert policies and cloud eval dashboards do not.
Google describes observability and governance as distinct platform responsibilities.
[Agent platform architecture](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/agents).

## Terraform, delivery and shutdown ownership

Keep this client's root/state separate from Scrapmarket. Pin providers, Python
dependencies, base/deployable image digests and approved release provenance. The
current Dockerfile's base tag is mutable, even though deployed images use digests.
Add a reviewed CI plan/apply flow with federation, restricted deployer permissions and
protected production approval. Artifact provenance/scanning and rollback are
release work, not guarantees supplied by an image digest alone.

The demo currently uses ignored **local state**. A multi-operator enterprise
deployment should use an access-controlled remote backend, locking/versioned
recovery and separate environment states. Google's Cloud Storage backend pattern
is an appropriate candidate. A retained state bucket has storage cost and should
live outside an ephemeral runtime's teardown dependency chain; approve that cost
exception before introducing it. It is not currently provisioned.
[Google Terraform state guidance](https://docs.cloud.google.com/docs/terraform/resource-management/store-state).

Current daily stop preserves project/APIs/IAM, removes billable gateway/image
resources and then unlinks billing. Protected project deletion is deliberately
blocked. Any new SQL database, memory store, secret, log sink or evaluation artifact
store needs Terraform ownership, startup/stop behavior, retention and verification.
An enterprise client's HA/backup/retention requirements can impose a persistent
cost floor; the local city's zero-cloud-cost development mode remains available.

## Delivery sequence and client demonstration

| Step | Scope | Acceptance evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Preserve local baseline | Versioned roles, business rules, queues and scenarios | Current isolation/regression receipts remain reproducible without credentials |
| 2. Harden paid decisions | Local durable request/result phases implemented; next: gateway-wide monetary admission and supervisor recovery | Local crash/duplicate/timeout checks plus future measured p95 and controller recovery; no double business effect |
| 3. Pilot one ADK role | Same approved tools and role contract, smallest passing model, explicit deployment identity | Same safety suite plus held-out quality/latency/cost comparison |
| 4. Select GCP hosting/governance | Cloud Run or managed runtime; networking, identity, memory and Terraform coverage based on client constraints | Reviewed threat/data-flow model, least-privilege negative tests and complete stop/retention inventory |
| 5. Operate and promote | Shadow evaluation, explicitly assigned canary, rollback and incident ownership | Agreed business/quality/SLO/cost gates and a signed-off handover |

In a walkthrough, show one order's queue lineage, authenticated scope, reservation,
selective memory, physical handoff and eval result. Then show the optional GCP
request boundary, caller/runtime identities, actual model-vs-policy response and
usage. Finish with the Terraform plan/parked status and the gaps above. This
demonstrates engineering decisions and evidence without presenting the demo as an
already production-certified enterprise agent platform.
